The Dourado (Salminus brasiliensis) is a large, migratory characid that supports important fisheries across the Paraná-Paraguay River basin. Field studies have documented that females can achieve a maximum recorded body size of 103 centimeters [Li = 103 centimeters] in total length, though individuals exceeding 80 centimeters are now increasingly rare due to historical overfishing. Males are considerably smaller than females, a pattern of sexual size dimorphism that is reflected in their respective asymptotic masses; while a large female can attain a maximum wet weight of 34 kilograms [Wwi = 34 kilograms], the maximum wet weight for males reaches only 25 kilograms [Wwi = 25 kilograms]. This pronounced difference in body size has implications for reproductive output, as larger females can carry substantially greater fecundities. The species is iteroparous, with spawning migrations triggered by seasonal floods and rising water temperatures, and the onset of sexual maturity is tied to a specific body length rather than to chronological age alone, a life-history trait common among potamodromous Neotropical fishes.

Reproductive biology in this species has been characterized under controlled conditions. At a water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], females produce approximately 2 million eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2 million eggs per year], a fecundity that reflects their large body size and high investment in pelagic egg production. Each spawning event releases between 500,000 and 1,000,000 eggs that are broadcast into the water column, where they undergo external fertilisation and develop as free-floating ichthyoplankton. The incubation period is brief, typically lasting from 12 to 18 hours before eclosion occurs, releasing yolk-sac larvae that are initially endotrophic. The onset of exogenous feeding occurs approximately three days after hatching, at which point the prolarvae begin to consume microcrustaceans and rotifers. This rapid transition from lecithotrophy to active feeding is critical for larval survival and is strongly influenced by thermal conditions, with the 21 °C [T = 21 °C] regime representing a common mean temperature during the early spring spawning season in the upper Paraná basin.

The age at which females achieve full reproductive capacity has been linked to the attainment of a total length at puberty of 37 centimeters [Lp = 37 centimeters]. Individuals reach this length between their second and third year of life in wild populations, depending on local growth rates and food availability. At this threshold, vitellogenesis begins and the fish become capable of participating in the annual spawning migrations. Males mature at a slightly smaller body size, though the length criterion remains similar. The wet weight at birth is extremely low, with recently hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of roughly two millimeters. This small initial mass places the larvae in the lower range of values documented for characid species and imposes a tight constraint on the duration of the endotrophic period; if exogenous prey is not encountered within three to five days following mouth opening, starvation-induced mortality becomes inevitable.

Longevity data for Salminus brasiliensis have been compiled from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimation. In the wild, the oldest documented individuals have been recorded at approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] of age under the thermal conditions typical of the Paraná basin (21 °C [T = 21 °C] mean annual water temperature), though most harvested fish are considerably younger, typically between 4 and 8 years old. Males appear to exhibit slightly shorter lifespans than females, a pattern that may be linked to the energetic costs of repeated spawning migrations. The maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] is consistent with values reported for other large-bodied South American characiforms and reflects a relatively slow life-history pace for a teleost of this size at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. Senescent individuals show reduced gonadal output and increased susceptibility to parasitism, particularly by branchiuran crustaceans, before eventual post-reproductive mortality occurs.

Habitat preferences of the Dourado are closely tied to the main channels of large rivers and the lower reaches of major tributaries, where fast-flowing, well-oxygenated water supports their high metabolic demands. Adults are piscivorous, preying primarily on characins, catfish, and even small cichlids, and they employ a striking ambush strategy using their powerful caudal fin to accelerate from cover. The species undertakes long-distance upstream migrations of several hundred kilometers during the austral spring to spawn in headwater regions, with the timing of these movements synchronized to the rising hydrograph. The 34 kilograms [Wwi = 34 kilograms] maximum wet weight recorded for females is exceptional among South American characins and gives the Dourado its reputation as the "tiger of the rivers." Conservation concerns are significant, as dam construction has fragmented critical migratory corridors and overfishing has reduced the average body size of spawning stocks, raising questions about the long-term viability of populations that now rely on a diminishing number of unobstructed river reaches.
